implementation_notes: ASP.NET Core gives the Action role directly: app.MapGet("/users/{id}", handler) registers exactly one delegate per method and route, the delegate receives parameters bound from the request instead of the raw HttpContext, and the Responder role is the returned IResult - TypedResults.Ok/BadRequest/NotFound, which also carry the OpenAPI metadata - or a plain object the framework serialises. Keep the domain in a DI-injected service that never receives HttpContext. The classic responder class is only justified when one action must answer in several content types, where a mapper or a per-format responder pays for itself.
pitfalls: Injecting HttpContext (or capturing it in the delegate) re-couples the action to the request; bind parameters instead so the handler stays testable.
Async delegates must return Task<IResult>: a void-returning or fire-and-forget handler turns domain errors into 500s with no response shape.
Minimal-API delegates are called per request, so a captured singleton that keeps per-request state is a concurrency bug.

variants.name: FastEndpoints endpoint class (REPR)
variants.idiom_name: FastEndpoints endpoint class per route (Configure + HandleAsync)
variants.implementation_notes: FastEndpoints is the class-per-endpoint realization of the same split and calls it REPR (Request-Endpoint-Response): each operation is its own Endpoint<TRequest, TResponse> class, Configure() declares the verb and route, HandleAsync() is the Action, and the strongly typed response DTO or an explicit status call is the Responder. Choose it over minimal APIs when DI, validation, OpenAPI generation and per-endpoint conventions should be uniform across hundreds of endpoints; choose the delegate form when the endpoint is one function and a class is overhead.
pitfalls: Endpoints are registered by assembly scanning: a class that is not discovered (wrong assembly, missing app.UseFastEndpoints) fails at runtime, not at compile time.
Putting business rules in Configure() or in the request DTO's validators mixes the Action and Domain roles.
SendAsync must be awaited; an unawaited send returns a response that may never be written.
